# Diagnosing Intermittent No-Start Conditions on a VW Jetta: Why "Wait Until It Dies Again" Isn't an Answer

When a vehicle exhibits intermittent symptomsâspecifically, refusing to start after sitting but igniting immediately after a jump start or a period of idlingâthe standard diagnostic approach often stalls. Dealerships frequently advise waiting for the issue to become constant before attempting repairs. This strategy assumes that a permanent failure state is required to isolate a faulty component, but it ignores the physics of transient electrical faults and parasitic draws. In the case of a 2013 VW Jetta S 2.0L with a three-year-old battery history, this advice can lead to unnecessary delays and wasted resources.

The specific symptom profile describedâcranking without combustion, resolving after a jump start, and failing again after short rest periodsâpoints strongly toward an electrical continuity or voltage regulation issue rather than a mechanical failure of the engine itself. The fact that the car runs fine for two weeks between incidents suggests the primary charging system is functional; otherwise, the alternator would likely fail to maintain charge over such durations.

### The Voltage Regulation Threshold

The update noting multimeter readings between 13.98V and 14.40V while running provides critical data. A healthy 12V lead-acid battery charging system should regulate output between 13.5V and 14.7V. Since the Jetta's alternator is operating within this acceptable range, we can rule out a failing voltage regulator or a broken alternator diode set that would cause immediate under-voltage conditions.

However, the car's inability to start after sitting indicates that the resting voltage is dropping below the threshold required for the Engine Control Unit (ECU) and fuel injectors to operate correctly. Modern ECUs often require at least 10V to enter "safe start" mode or manage the ignition coil firing sequences. If the battery rests at 12.8V or lower after a short idle period, the ECU may disable fuel injection or prevent spark generation until voltage recovers.

### Parasitic Drain and Battery Age

The timeline of the battery replacement is the most significant variable here. The original battery was three years old when it failed. Lead-acid batteries typically have a service life of 3 to 5 years, but high-temperature environments or frequent short trips can degrade them prematurely. When you replaced this unit with a new one, the system reset, explaining the week-long stability.

The recurring issue after just an hour of sitting suggests a parasitic drain that is slightly higher than normal but not enough to kill the battery in 24 hours. A typical parasitic draw should be between 50mA and 85mA. If a short circuit exists in an aftermarket accessory, a failing ECU module (common on VWs of this era due to voltage spikes), or corroded grounds, the draw could sit at 150mA to 200mA.

To diagnose this without waiting for a total failure, you can perform a load test while the car is off:
1. Connect a high-quality digital multimeter in series with the negative battery terminal.
2. Ensure all doors are closed and windows are fully up.
3. Wait 15 minutes for modules to enter sleep mode.
4. Check the reading.

If the current exceeds 100mA, you have identified a parasitic drain. The next step is disconnecting fuses one by one until the amperage drops, isolating the circuit causing the bleed-off. This method avoids the "wait for death" strategy and actively hunts down the leak.

### Grounding and Connection Integrity

The source material mentions that cleaning connections did not solve the problem. While surface oxidation is a common culprit on older vehicles, deep corrosion within the terminal posts or at the chassis ground points can cause intermittent high resistance. When the engine cranks, it creates a massive voltage drop across these poor connections. If the voltage at the starter motor drops below 9V during cranking, the engine will spin but won't fire.

A jump start works because it bypasses the compromised battery terminals and provides sufficient amperage directly to the starter and ignition system, temporarily masking the high-resistance ground path. The car then starts on its own after sitting longer because the alternator has had time to recharge the battery sufficiently to overcome the voltage drop at the bad connection.

### Why Dealership Replacements May Fail

The dealership's suggestion to replace five different components is a classic "parts swap" approach that treats symptoms, not causes. Replacing the ignition coil pack, crankshaft position sensor, or fuel pump will yield no results if the root cause is an electrical supply issue. The ECU cannot control the injectors if it lacks the minimum voltage threshold to trigger them.

Instead of waiting for a constant failure, use a load tester or a professional battery analyzer to check the Cold Cranking Amps (CCA) and reserve capacity of the new battery. If the CCA drops significantly after only a few weeks of use, the battery may be sensitive to the engine's high draw during cold starts, even if resting voltage looks normal. Alternatively, inspect the negative battery cable from the chassis ground strap to the engine block; a loose or corroded ground strap is a frequent cause of "no-start after sitting" scenarios that mimic alternator failure.

By focusing on parasitic drain measurement and grounding integrity rather than replacing sensors, you can resolve this intermittent issue without further delay.
